one_liner: C++ port of Intel's 3-way crc32q+pclmulqdq CRC-32C kernel that also runs on 32-bit x86; ~11x faster than slicing-by-8.
what_it_does: A combined benchmark and code collection of eight CRC-32C (Castagnoli) implementations in namespace `logging`. All share the signature `uint32_t fn(uint32_t crc, const void* data, size_t length)`, and the caller wraps them with crc32cInit() (0xFFFFFFFF) and crc32cFinish() (~crc). The project's own contribution is crc32cIntelC, a port of Intel's crc_iscsi_v_pcl.asm to C++ with GCC builtins and inline asm, which also compiles for 32-bit x86 (the Intel Edison target). It is not packaged: the Makefile builds only a test binary and a benchmark binary, and you copy the .cc/.h files you need.
how_it_is_fast: The SSE4.2 crc32 instruction has 3-cycle latency but single-cycle throughput. Above 216 bytes the buffer is therefore cut into three equal segments of up to 1024 bytes (128 eight-byte words), and three independent crc32q streams run interleaved, unrolled with Duff's device. The three partial CRCs are then merged: two of them are carry-less-multiplied (pclmulqdq) by precomputed x^n mod P constants from a block-size-indexed table and XOR-folded into the third. This is the method of Intel's 2011 whitepaper 'Fast CRC Computation for iSCSI Polynomial Using CRC32 Instruction' (Gopal et al.). On 32-bit builds each crc32q becomes two crc32l, and the merge uses movd/pextrd.
when_to_use: CRC-32C (iSCSI, ext4, Btrfs polynomial) on 32-bit i686 builds with SSE4.2 and PCLMULQDQ, such as Intel Edison or legacy 32-bit software, where the alternative is slicing-by-8 or a crc32l loop: 8.8x over SlicingBy8 on 32-bit Edison.
Buffers of roughly 1-8 KiB on 64-bit Haswell/Skylake-class desktop cores without AVX-512: about 2.7x a single-stream crc32q loop at 4 KiB on an i7-4770.
You want a readable C-level reference of Intel's 3-way crc32+pclmul CRC-32C algorithm to study or port, instead of the yasm assembly.
Comparing CRC-32C implementations: crc32cbench sweeps 16 B to 8 KiB, aligned and misaligned, across all eight bundled variants.
when_not_to_use: zlib/gzip/PNG/Ethernet CRC-32: it computes CRC-32C only, and issue #3 is a user tripped up by exactly this difference.
Silvermont-class Atoms (Edison in 64-bit mode, NUC E3815): the author's chart shows every 3-way path (Adler, IntelC, IntelAsm) slower there than the plain Hardware64 loop.

Small or mid-size messages: at 216 B and below it is a single crc32q stream. In a third-party i7-8665U run, throughput fell from about 24.7 GB/s at 128 B to about 16 GB/s at 256 B, right after the 3-way path starts.

Modern AVX-512/VPCLMULQDQ servers or aarch64: the corsix fast-crc32 README measures the pure three-way crc32 approach at about 15-24 GB/s, against 25-97 GB/s for its fusion and VPCLMULQDQ kernels. There is no ARM port.
MSVC or long-term maintenance needs: it relies on GCC __builtin_ia32_crc32* builtins, GNU inline asm and <cpuid.h>, and has been untouched since 2017.

integration.form: source-drop (crc32intelc.cc, logging/crc32intelc.h and the K constant table in crc32inteltable.cc; the Makefile only builds the test and benchmark executables)
integration.dependencies: none for IntelC; yasm only for the IntelAsm variant; the tests use the bundled stupidunit
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented. g++ with -msse4.2 -mpclmul (the chart shows g++ 6.3 and 7.2). The code is C++ (.cc) with GNU inline asm.
integration.platforms: x86 only (i686 and x86-64), requiring SSE4.2 and PCLMULQDQ; the IntelAsm variant is 64-bit only
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The kernels are pure functions over const tables, but the global `logging::crc32c` pointer rewrites itself on its first call with no synchronization.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same (crc, ptr, len) shape as typical slicing-by-8 CRC-32C code, but the caller must apply the 0xFFFFFFFF init and final inversion, the symbols live in namespace logging, and it is not a replacement for zlib's crc32().

gotchas: The auto-dispatch pointer `logging::crc32c` (detectBestCRC32C) picks Hardware64/Hardware32 on any SSE4.2 CPU and never IntelC. It also checks only SSE4.2, not PCLMULQDQ. Call crc32cIntelC directly and do your own feature check.
The kernels do no pre- or post-inversion. Without crc32cInit() and crc32cFinish() the results will not match standard CRC-32C test vectors (e.g. 0xE3069283 for '123456789').

The 32-bit CombineCRC inline asm writes to operands declared only as inputs (crc32l into crc2's register, pextrd into %1), which GCC's inline-asm rules forbid. It passed the repo's tests with g++ 6.3/7.2 but could miscompile under newer compilers.
The crc32cIntelAsm wrapper casts the size_t length to int, so that variant breaks on buffers of 2 GiB or more (IntelC keeps size_t).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over fast-crc32 (corsix) only for 32-bit x86 or pre-AVX-512 Intel desktop chips where you want one small hand-written C++ file with no generator step; on 64-bit x86 corsix's fusion kernels supersede it and also cover aarch64. crc-fast offers runtime dispatch and many CRC widths, and crc32fast is Rust and computes zlib CRC-32, so neither replaces this for a C/C++ CRC-32C drop-in on 32-bit.
verified_claims_summary: crc32cbench hashes one 4096-byte, 8-byte-aligned buffer repeatedly (so it stays in cache) and reports the median of 5 trials in MiB/s. The builds used g++ 6.3/7.2 with -O3 -flto -msse4.2 -mpclmul. On a 64-bit Haswell i7-4770, IntelC reached roughly 27,000 MiB/s (read off the log chart): 2.7x a single-stream crc32q loop, about 11x Intel's slicing-by-8 tables, about 1.2x Mark Adler's 3-way SSE4.2 code, and level with the Intel asm it ports. It was 8.8x slicing-by-8 on 32-bit Edison but lost to Hardware64 on 64-bit Silvermont Atoms.
status_note: Abandoned since 2017-11-01 (12 commits, no open issues, none of its 18 forks active after 2020), but small and permissively licensed (MIT-style BSD-3 LICENSE, with Zlib-licensed headers on crc32intelc.cc and crc32adler.cc) and easy to vendor. It was last known to work with g++ 7.2.
